Checkpoints: shared arguments, personal data and database tables

Source: R/report.R
checkpoints.Rd

The ensure_*() functions are checkpoints: each states a rule about the data, warns or aborts with the offending rows when it is broken, and returns data invisibly, so it can sit in the middle of a pipeline. Most rules are about structure; ensure_none(), ensure_all() and ensure_empty() take any rule dplyr can express. This page documents what they share.

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble, a database table (dbplyr, e.g. DuckDB) or an Arrow table or dataset; see Database and Arrow tables.

success_msg

Message shown when the rule holds. If NULL (default), it is "Check passed: <message>" when warn_msg or abort_msg is given, so the console names every check that ran, and a description of the check otherwise.

warn_msg

Message shown when the rule is broken and no abort_msg is set. Defaults to a description of the check.

abort_msg

If provided, cli::cli_abort() is called with this message when the rule is broken. If NULL (default), a warning is issued instead.

Details

The failure message

A failure is laid out in the same order by every structure check: what broke, the number of rows, counts that show the pattern (exact copies against copies that differ, units, periods, codes, the columns that vary), the first rows, and the next step. Five rows do not show whether 40,000 duplicates are one year or the whole table; the counts do, and show fewer personal data. They are computed only when the check fails.

The next step is code to copy, with the column names filled in: the call to wrap in violations(), and a fix where one is unambiguous, such as dplyr::distinct() for exact copies or merge_spells() for overlapping spells. Where a fix takes a choice the package cannot make, such as which of two differing copies to keep, the code has a hole in it, <column>. When the console is too narrow for every column, the preview keeps the key, the diagnostic column and the columns that explain the failure, and names the others.

The offending rows are deliberately not kept in the session afterwards: on a population register a failed check can hold millions of rows, and they would stay in memory until the next failure. Messages are shown literally: braces are not interpolated. Diagnostic columns such as dupid, missing, overlap_id, gap, outside and reason receive a numeric suffix when their name is already in the input (for example dupid.1). All original columns keep their names and values.

A failed check signals a condition of class inshape_failure (a warning or an error) that carries the offending rows in its violations field. violations() catches it and returns the rows, to look at all of them in the session:

dups <- violations(ensure_unique(persons, cpr))

Personal data

inshape is made for interactive review of registers, at the console in the environment where the data lives. The offending rows of a check are personal data: they hold the key, often a cpr number, and every other column of the rows. inshape therefore writes nothing to disk, neither the rows nor a log of the checks, and keeps nothing after a check:

  • The message shows the number of rows, counts that show their pattern (per year, per code, per column), and the first 5 of them at the console. Output that is kept, such as a rendered report or a shared screen, keeps them too, so run the checks at the console.

  • The condition carries the rows in memory, until it is caught, by violations() for one, or dropped. Whether any of them are stored, and where, is for the analysis and its data agreement to decide, not the package.

To keep the rows, save them yourself, from what violations() returns:

violations(ensure_none(sales, amount < 0)) |>
  data.table::fwrite("negative_amounts.csv")

Speed

Every check, and every describe_*() function, starts by compressing the key columns to integer ids with a compiled, multi-threaded hash, without sorting them. Nothing is kept between calls, so each check compresses its columns anew; even so, ensure_unique() on 5 million rows takes about 0.2 seconds (see the benchmarks in the repository). The engine uses as many threads as data.table, set with data.table::setDTthreads().

Database and Arrow tables

Every checkpoint also takes a database table from dbplyr, such as a DuckDB table, and an Arrow table or dataset, and checks it where it lives. The violation set is built as a query, and only its size and the preview rows are fetched into R, so a check on a register too large for memory still works. Arrow data is queried through DuckDB with arrow::to_duckdb(). This needs the dbplyr package, and duckdb for Arrow.

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), "register.duckdb")

dplyr::tbl(con, "persons") |>
  ensure_unique(cpr, year) |>
  ensure_balanced(cpr, year, gaps_only = TRUE)

A checkpoint returns the table it was given, still unevaluated, so the pipeline continues in the database. On a failure the condition's violations field, and so violations(), holds the violation set as a query: collect() it to get the rows. Two things differ from data frames, because a database table has no row order: ensure_unique() numbers dupid in the order of the key instead of first appearance, and spells starting on the same day are ordered by their end in ensure_no_overlap().

The describe_*() functions take database and Arrow tables too. Each summary is computed in the database with grouped counts, and only those counts are fetched, so describing a register costs a few small queries whatever its size. The numbers are the same as in memory, which the tests check. Two differences: participation patterns with the same count at the cut of describe_panel()'s patterns may be chosen differently, and in describe_changes() the keys that came, went or changed stay queries, to collect().

See also

ensure_unique(), ensure_complete(), ensure_balanced(), ensure_no_overlap(), ensure_no_gaps(), ensure_valid_spells(), ensure_constant(), ensure_within(), ensure_codes() and ensure_matched() for the structure, ensure_panel(), ensure_spells() and ensure_lookup() for the common ones in one call, ensure_none(), ensure_all(), ensure_empty() and tally_violations() for rules of your own, and violations() for the rows that break one.
